title: Multiplexed invoker patterns and polyglot SDK samples for streaming tools & structured outputs
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Define and ship a lightweight, backward-compatible SDK pattern that lets clients open a single streaming call and receive multiplexed frames for: model token deltas, tool/function invocations, structured output events (JSON schema fragments), and non-critical telemetry. Deliver TypeScript, Python, and Go examples and a migration guide for existing SDKs.
background: We currently have multiple competing streaming semantics across SDKs: incremental token streams, tool callbacks as separate channels, and structured output fragments sent as ad-hoc events. This makes it hard for client apps to compose multiple tools with low latency and deterministic ordering. Customers building complex agent-style flows want a single, efficient connection that carries model output, tool events, and structured payloads without per-tool HTTP requests.
proposal:
Introduce a multiplexed frame protocol on top of our streaming API. Key elements:
- Frame envelope: {id, kind, seq, payload, resume_token?} where kind in [model_delta, tool_call, tool_result, structured_fragment, meta].
- Ordering guarantees: per-id seq monotonicity; global interleaving allowed to reduce latency.
- Resume semantics: resume_token for persistent sessions; clients can reattach and request missing seq ranges.
- Backpressure: client-driven window (credits) to avoid OOM on constrained clients; runtime enforces per-connection memory caps.
- Polyglot surface: provide ergonomic interfaces in TypeScript (async iterator + event emitter), Python (async generator + callbacks), Go (channel+context) that map directly to frames.
- Compatibility layer: a thin adapter in each language that exposes a deprecated single-stream delta view for existing clients (so older SDKs continue receiving token deltas) while new clients opt-into multiplexing via a header or param.
samples:
Python example:

# simplified pseudo-example
from redwood import create_multiplex_stream
stream = await create_multiplex_stream(model='rw-13b')
async for frame in stream:
    if frame['kind'] == 'model_delta':
        print(frame['payload']['text'], end='', flush=True)
    elif frame['kind'] == 'tool_call':
        result = await my_tool.invoke(frame['payload'])
        await stream.send({'id': frame['id'], 'kind': 'tool_result', 'payload': {'result': result}})
    elif frame['kind'] == 'structured_fragment':
        assembler.add(frame['id'], frame['seq'], json.loads(frame['payload']))
    else:
        logger.debug('meta', frame['payload'])
implementation_plan: Design review: finalize frame envelope and field names (one day).
Runtime: implement multiplex encoder/decoder and per-connection memory window (3 days).
SDKs: implement adapters for TS/Python/Go, plus deprecation adapter for old streaming API (4 days).
Docs: write migration guide with examples and a troubleshooting section for state reassembly (1 day).
QA: integration tests + fuzzing for resume and seq gaps; perf test for latency and memory under high concurrency (2 days).
Rollout: opt-in header 'X-Redwood-Multiplex: 1' for two weeks, then enable by default behind feature flag after client opt-in metrics look good.
acceptance_criteria: TypeScript, Python, and Go SDKs expose a documented multiplexed stream interface and shipping examples.
Existing single-stream token-delta clients continue to work without code changes when the compatibility header is not set.
Resume semantics validated: reattach within 5 minutes and recover missing seqs in < 200ms for typical session sizes.
Backpressure mechanism prevents unbounded memory growth in client SDKs; tested with 1000 concurrent simulated clients.
Integration tests covering tool_call -> tool_result roundtrip and structured_fragment reassembly pass in CI.
Design doc and migration guide published (confluence link in links) and engaged with SDK maintainers for review.
updates: 2026-03-11: Kickoff meeting done. Decided to use per-id seq instead of global seq to simplify reassembly for long-running tool results.
2026-03-12: Runtime encoder/decoder spike completed; initial memory window approach implemented and instrumentation added. API still under review by SDK owners.
2026-03-13: TS SDK prototype landed in draft PR and requested feedback from DX and SDK teams; noted need for ergonomic reassembly utility for structured fragments.
Blocking: need decision on resume token lifetime (recommendation: 10 min sliding window) — action: security/product to sign off by 2026-03-15.
Review feedback: SDK owners requested optional convenience adapter that exposes a token-only async iterator for simple clients; added to acceptance criteria.
